blocks.text: I built a custom agent on @tread_fi that currently ranks number one for volume generated through hires on the agent marketplace — 11.3m in volume across 76 hires. I wrote no code to do it. I described what I wanted in plain English, and it has been running that description on other people's accounts ever since, on exchanges I am not even trading.

This article is the complete walkthrough for building one yourself: describe your strategy in plain English, your @tread_fi custom agent trades it, and once the builder fee share goes live, it pays you when others hire it.

Most of what gets called an "AI agent" in crypto is a chatbot with a token attached. TreadFi custom agents are something different, and the difference is worth understanding before you build one.

A custom agent is a set of execution rules you write down. You describe what the agent should look for, what it should do when it finds it, how it should size, where it should stop, and when it should do nothing. TreadFi turns that description into a working agent that runs on live markets through the same execution engine institutions use.

Then comes the part nobody else in this space is doing: you can list that agent publicly. Other people hire it. They run it on their own exchange accounts using API, with their own capital and their own margin, and it executes your rules for them. The volume they generate pays fees to Tread.

Fee sharing with agent builders is not switched on yet — it is a feature the team has said is coming, and according to them the share to the creator can go up to 80%. Nothing is being paid out today. What is live today is everything else: building the agent, listing it, being hired, and accumulating a real usage record while the marketplace is still small.

That last part is why this is worth doing now rather than later. Good traders have always had a distribution problem — the only way to monetise a process was to trade it yourself, sell a course, or take on other people's money. An agent marketplace is a fourth path, and it doesn't require managing a single dollar of anyone else's capital. When the fee share does arrive, the agents with hires and volume behind them are the ones positioned for it.

I have been using TreadFi since the early days and building custom agents since the feature launched. This guide covers everything: what these agents can do, what you can build, exactly how to create your first one step by step, how to promote it, how to edit it, how hires work, and the caveats nobody tells you about.

If you don't have a TreadFi account yet, you'll need one to follow along. You can open one here: https://app.tread.fi/referral/59S1TB1X — it gives you no discount and costs you nothing extra. It just sends a small share my way. Use it if you found this useful.
Part 1 — What a custom agent actually is
A custom agent is preset rules for execution.

Not a signal service. Not a prediction machine. Not a black box that guesses direction. You define the logic — the scan, the filter, the entry trigger, the sizing, the stop, the target, the conditions under which it should stand down — and the agent carries it out continuously without you watching.
Three things separate this from a bot you'd script yourself:
It runs on institutional execution infrastructure. You are not writing exchange API calls or worrying about order types. The agent has access to Tread's full algo suite and order management layer.
It runs unattended. Once the rules are set, the agent scans, waits, enters, manages and exits on its own. You are not sitting in front of a chart waiting for a level.
It is portable. This is the important one. Your agent is not locked to your account. You can publish it, and other people can hire it and run it on theirs.
What an agent can actually watch
This is the part most people underestimate, so be clear on it before you start writing rules.

Any indicator, at any threshold you name. RSI, EMA, ADX, Bollinger Band width, whatever you work off — you tell the agent which indicator, on which timeframe, and at what number it should act. "Enter when 5m RSI is between 30 and 40." "Only trade pairs where 1h EMA20 is above EMA50 is above EMA200." "Skip anything with ADX under 20." The agent reads the live data and holds fire until your number prints.

Time windows. You can tell it which hours to run and which hours to stay flat. If you know your strategy dies during the London open or through US data releases, say so, and the agent will avoid those windows without you setting an alarm.

Continuous monitoring, and it wakes itself. You do not have to be online, and you do not have to ask it to go and check. It keeps checking on its own and comes alive the moment your conditions are met. That's the whole difference between a rule you wrote down and a rule that actually gets executed — most setups are missed not because the trader didn't know the level, but because they weren't watching at 3am.

You describe all of this in plain English. You do not write code, you do not configure a trigger builder, and you do not maintain a script on a server somewhere. You write what you want, and the agent handles the watching.

That is worth restating, because it is the thing that makes an agent different from a bot: you supply the judgement, the agent supplies the attention. Attention is the resource every discretionary trader actually runs out of.
Part 2 — Where this is heading: the builder fee share
Here is the loop the platform is building toward.

You build an agent. You promote it to the marketplace. Someone hires it, connects their own exchange account using API, gives it margin, and lets it run. Every order it places for them routes through Tread and pays Tread a builder fee. A share of that fee goes back to the person who wrote the rules.

To be clear about the current state: this is not live yet. No creator is being paid a fee share today. It is a feature the team has said is coming, and per the team the share can reach up to 80%. Treat the number as their stated intent, not as something you can go and earn this afternoon.
What makes it worth understanding now is what it does to incentives once it lands:
A trader with a genuinely good execution process gets a way to monetise it that does not involve managing money, raising a fund, or selling a course.
The reward would be continuous rather than one-off — paid for as long as people keep using the agent and generating volume through it.
The incentive points in the right direction. Agents that work get hired repeatedly; agents that don't get abandoned. Usage, not marketing, is what would pay.

It is a better deal than vaults or copy trading for the person hiring, too. With a vault you hand over capital. With copy trading you mirror someone's positions blind. With a custom agent, the capital stays in your account, and you can tweak the inputs — exchange, pairs, margin, risk per trade — while the logic stays intact.

I keep saying this and I'll say it here: nobody else in crypto is building this. There are AI agent narratives everywhere and almost no AI agent marketplaces where the agents actually execute, actually generate measurable volume, and are set up to pay the builder for it. This is the first one I have seen going after that loop end to end.

The practical takeaway for a builder reading this: the work you do now — an agent that people actually hire and run — is the position. It costs nothing to list, and the record it accumulates is the thing that will matter when the share turns on.
Part 3 — What you can build: three examples from my own account

You can currently build a maximum of three custom agents per account. That cap will presumably move, but for now it forces you to be deliberate about what you make. Here is what I built with my three.
1. Nooru's Market Maker Agent
Runs a market-making bot on any exchange TreadFi supports, according to my rule set.

The user does almost nothing. They hire it, point it at an exchange, give it margin, and the agent takes over — it pulls the top pairs by volume, runs a regime check before it starts, market makes while conditions are favourable, and pauses itself when they turn. It skips volatile hours and red-level news windows on its own.
Current numbers: 11.3m in volume across 74 hires.

That is the clearest proof I have that this model works. Seventy-four people who don't know me, running my rules on their own accounts, generating volume I never had to babysit.

Link to the agent where you can hire this: https://app.tread.fi/agents/marketplace/60164439dbd7431a84f610ede6130ec3
2. Top funding shorts agent

A strategy agent. It scans a given exchange for the five highest positive-funding pairs and shorts them according to a set rule set — aggregate stop loss, flat everything on stop, take profit after 24 hours, then repeat.

The logic behind it: pairs with extreme positive funding are usually crowded longs, and crowded positioning tends to mean-revert. The agent targets exactly that condition, mechanically, every day, without me deciding anything.
Anyone who wants to run that strategy can hire the agent and apply it. That is what a strategy agent is — a trade idea packaged so someone else can execute it properly.
3. HTF trend continuation agent
Scans every pair on a chosen exchange for a clean higher-timeframe trend, then watches the lower timeframe for a pullback into that trend and enters on set rules.

This is the one I will use as the worked example below, because it is the most instructive: it has a scan, a filter, a user choice, a continuous monitor, an entry trigger, a fixed risk model, and a re-validation step.

There is a second use for an agent like this that most people haven't clocked yet: connect a prop firm challenge account and let the agent run the strategy on it. Challenges are pass/fail on discipline more than on ideas — mechanical rules, fixed risk, no revenge trades. That is exactly what an agent is good at.

Currently treadfi agents can trade challege accounts from @ProprXYZ . This was a recent integration on treadfi. 

Propr ref if you havent yet started - https://app.propr.xyz/r/nooru
Part 4 — The state of the marketplace right now

Be honest about where we are: there are hundreds of agents listed, and it is hard to tell which ones are any good.

We are in the trial phase. Anyone can list, listing is free, and a lot of what is up there was promoted in the hope of airdrop credit rather than because it does something useful. Filtering signal from spam is genuinely difficult today.

That changes when the TREAD token arrives. The plan is that users will stake TREAD to release custom agents — you spend staked tokens to put an agent on the marketplace. That single change removes most of the spam, because a listing will cost something. What survives will be agents people actually thought about.
If you are building now, this is the window. Getting hires and a volume record on the board before the marketplace gets crowded with serious builders is worth more than it will be later.
Part 5 — How to create a custom agent, step by step
Step 1: Open the builder
Go to https://app.tread.fi/agents/new and click Start from alpha.

You will see a describe box, and below it a few starting templates — Watch and alert, Market maker, Delta neutral. Templates are fine for a first look, but the whole point of a custom agent is the describe box. That is where you write your own flow.
Step 2: Write the spec
Describe the entire agent flow in the describe box. Plain language works, but structured plain language works far better.
A good spec answers, in order:
What does the agent need from the user before it starts?
What is the filter that defines the universe?
Who picks the pairs — the agent or the user?
What exactly triggers an entry?
How is the position sized, stopped and taken profit on?
What does it re-check before it acts?

You do not have to write this cold. Use Claude or GPT to draft your spec — describe your strategy conversationally, ask it to turn that into a structured agent specification, then paste the result here.
Here is the exact spec I used to build an agent that longs a 5m pullback while the 1h higher timeframe is trending:

Agent spec: HTF trend continuation, 5m entries

1. Setup — user inputs
Before scanning, collect from the user:
- Exchange to scan
- Max loss per trade
- Margin to allocate per position

2. Higher-timeframe trend filter
Scan all pairs on the selected exchange and keep only those where:
- 1h: EMA20 > EMA50 > EMA200 (uptrend) or EMA20 < EMA50 < EMA200 (downtrend)
- Daily: price above EMA20 (uptrend) or below EMA20 (downtrend)
- RSI above 70 on the trend timeframe, confirming momentum

3. Pair selection
Present the filtered list of trending pairs to the user. The user picks one or
multiple pairs to monitor. No trades are placed on unselected pairs.

4. Continuous 5m monitoring
For each selected pair, watch the 5m chart for a pullback/extension entry
against the HTF direction bias:
- 5m RSI 30–40 → long entry (pullback in an uptrend)
- 5m RSI 70–80 → short entry (extension in a downtrend)
The agent keeps scanning continuously until an entry condition triggers or
the user stops it.

5. Trade execution
- Stop loss: 1%
- Take profit: 2%
- Position size derived from the user's stated max loss per trade and margin input

6. Re-validation
Before each entry, re-check that the HTF trend conditions in step 2 still hold.
If the pair has fallen out of trend, skip the signal and drop it from the
watchlist.

That is a simple example. Refine it with your own AI, tighten the numbers to your own methodology, and understand that the possibilities here go well beyond a trend filter — anything you can describe as a repeatable process is buildable.
Paste your spec into the describe section and click the up-arrow button. The agent starts drafting.
Step 3: Answer the follow-up questions
Once the initial draft is done, the builder shows you what it built — the capability groups, how many order actions and read actions it granted, and whether the agent can place orders.

It will usually come back with one or two open questions. Mine asked whether it should place the orders itself or just hand them to me. Answer in the box, click the up-arrow, and let it finish.

Then click Activate agent.
Your agent is now live for your own use.
Step 4: Understand Personality and Abilities
Two tabs sit next to Describe, and both matter.

Personality controls how the agent talks and how it introduces itself — expertise tags (which a Supervisor reads to decide what to route to it), voice scales, and an option to source a writing style from a public X handle.

Core, inside this section, is the important one. Core is the actual brain of your agent — the standing instruction set it operates from. This is where you go when you want to change how the agent behaves, and it is where most of your future edits will happen.
Part 6 — Promoting your agent to the marketplace
You can use your agent yourself as soon as it is activated. If you want other people to hire it, you have to promote it.
Click Promote from the top of the agent page. On the next screen, click Run AI review & promote to marketplace.

If this is your first agent, you will be asked to claim a public profile — a handle other users will see as the agent's author. Note what the dialog tells you: your handle and avatar replace your masked address on competition leaderboards, your competition wallets become publicly linked to that handle, and your market-maker volume, season ranks and competition wins become visible.
The AI review runs, and if it passes, your agent goes live as v1 with auto-generated version notes describing what it does.
Part 7 — Managing your agent
Manage Agents is your dashboard. It shows, per agent:
Attributed volume — the USD notional your listing plus your own source agent has generated
Your usage — turns per day
Your token usage — token consumption per day
Hire cohorts — active hires, grouped by hire date
Version history — every release, its date, its authority level, and the notes your hirers saw
This is where you find out whether your agent is actually being used, which is the only number that matters once it is listed.
Part 8 — Editing your agent (and the caveats)
There are two ways to change an agent, and you will end up using both.
Method 1 — refine in chat
Click on the edit  agent and type your change in plain language in the Describe section. Something like "Change HTF filter to 4h instead of 1h." The preview updates as you go, then you save.
Method 2 — edit Core directly

Sometimes the chat refinement doesn't take. When that happens, I go to Personality → Core and make the change there directly. If I want to add a new behaviour, I write it into Core, hit Save, and the agent picks it up.
Two caveats you need to know

1. Changes do not apply to tasks that are already running. An edit only affects new tasks. Anything currently live on the old instruction set stays on the old instruction set until you stop it and start again.
2. Editing does not update your marketplace listing. Your hirers keep running the version they hired. To push your changes to them, go to Manage Agents → Publish new version, then Promote v2.

The promote dialog shows you a diff before anything ships: how many prompt lines changed, whether actions changed, whether order authority changed, and the AI-generated version notes your hirers will see. Promoting writes those notes and notifies everyone who hired the agent.
That versioning discipline is worth appreciating. Your hirers are never silently switched onto different logic — they get a note describing exactly what changed.
Part 9 — Using your agent
Prerequisite: connect and whitelist an exchange account
An agent cannot do anything until it has permission. You need a Tread UOA or a connected exchange account, and that account must be whitelisted for agent use with Trade access enabled.
If the account isn't whitelisted, the agent will load and greet you, but the chat stays locked — you will see "Chat unlocks once an account is whitelisted" with a Configure access button.
I've covered account connection and whitelisting in detail in a previous guide:

Start a session

Go to Start Session. Your custom agent appears in the list alongside Tread's own agents — Supervisor, Desk Trader, DN Bot, Market Maker and the rest. Click yours.

On the next screen you can either use one of the preset prompts the agent suggests, or type your own. The agent will ask for whatever inputs your spec told it to collect — in my example, exchange, max loss per trade and margin per position.
Then it runs.
Part 10 — Hiring agents (yours and other people's)
Go to Marketplace(https://app.tread.fi/agents/marketplace), search the agent name, click it, and click Hire agent.
You don't need to hire your own agent — you already have access to it. But this is how anyone else picks yours up, and how you pick up theirs.
Every agent you hire shows up under Manage Agents, and appears in your list when you click Start Session.
Two limits worth knowing:
There is no limit on how many agents you can hire.
There is a limit on how many custom agents you can create — currently three.
Part 11 — How to think about what you build
That is everything mechanical. The harder question is what to build.

An agent doesn't have to be a money-printing machine. Mine isn't. My market maker agent doesn't produce a green PnL every session, and it was never designed to. What it does is remove friction — it lets someone market make on any supported exchange without sitting in front of a screen deciding when conditions are right.
That is what got it 74 hires.
So the question to ask is not "what strategy would make the most money." It's "what part of my trading workflow would other people want to not do manually?"
Some directions worth exploring:
Execution agents — market making, delta neutral, TWAP-style entries, anything where the process matters more than the call
Strategy agents — your entry rules, packaged so someone else can run them properly
Screening agents — scan a universe on your criteria and surface only what qualifies
Monitoring agents — watch funding, ETF flows, social sentiment, unlock schedules, and report

It is just a tool. Explore it, and a lot of ideas will come. The builders who take it seriously in this window — before staking gates the listings and the marketplace fills up with people who've figured this out — are the ones who'll have a volume record and a hire count when it matters.
